Isaiah 1.audience: Isaiah son of Amoz spoke to Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1), roughly 740–700 BC. His first hearers were the people and rulers of Jerusalem.

culture.title: A lodge in a garden of cucumbers
culture.text: Farmers built small huts or booths in fields and vineyards to guard ripening crops. After harvest they were left standing alone—an image of Jerusalem isolated after invasion.

culture.title: Sacrifices without justice
culture.text: Rams, bullocks, new moons, and sabbaths were the regular worship of the temple. Isaiah says God rejects them when the worshippers' hands are "full of blood."

culture.title: Silver become dross
culture.text: Dross is the waste skimmed off in refining metal; wine "mixed with water" was watered down to cheat buyers.

Isaiah 2.audience: Isaiah 2:2–4 is nearly identical to Micah 4:1–3; the two prophets were contemporaries. Its first hearers knew Jerusalem as the mountain of the LORD's house.

culture.title: Swords into plowshares
culture.text: Iron was used for both weapons and farm tools. Reforging swords into plow blades and spears into pruning hooks pictures lasting peace. The words are carved on the Isaiah Wall across from United Nations headquarters in New York.

culture.title: Hiding in caves
culture.text: In times of invasion people fled to the limestone caves and clefts of the hills.

culture.title: Ships of Tarshish
culture.text: "Ships of Tarshish" were large merchant ships, symbols of wealth and pride.

Isaiah 3.audience: Isaiah warns Jerusalem's leaders and the wealthy women of the city of coming judgment.

culture.title: The finery of Zion's daughters
culture.text: The list of ornaments—anklets, cauls, crescent pendants, earrings, bracelets, veils, headdresses, perfume boxes, nose rings, and fine linen—is the most detailed list of women's jewelry and clothing in the Old Testament.

culture.title: Children as rulers
culture.text: When experienced leaders were killed or deported, inexperienced young men were left to rule.

Isaiah 4.audience: A short chapter promising cleansing and protection for those left in Zion after judgment.

culture.title: Seven women and one man
culture.text: After war killed many men, women would plead to be married simply to remove the shame of being unmarried and childless.

culture.title: Cloud and fire
culture.text: "A cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night" recalls the pillar that led Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21).

Isaiah 5.audience: Isaiah sings a song about a vineyard to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, then reveals that they are the vineyard (Isaiah 5:7).

culture.title: Building a vineyard
culture.text: A vineyard owner fenced the land, cleared stones, planted choice vines, built a watchtower, and cut a winepress into the rock.

culture.title: House joined to house
culture.text: Wealthy landowners bought up neighbors' fields until small farmers were driven off—forbidden by the law's land inheritance rules (Leviticus 25:23).

culture.title: Wordplay in Hebrew
culture.text: God looked for judgment (mishpat) and found oppression (mispach), for righteousness (tsedaqah) and found a cry (tse'aqah)—a pun lost in translation.

Isaiah 6.audience: Isaiah describes his call "in the year that king Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1), about 740 BC. Jesus and Paul quote the commission of verses 9–10 (Matthew 13:14–15; Acts 28:25–27).

culture.title: Seraphims
culture.text: Seraphim means ‘burning ones.’ This is the only place in the Bible where they appear as heavenly beings; the same word describes the "fiery serpents" of Numbers 21:6.

culture.title: A live coal from the altar
culture.text: Coals from the altar were used to burn incense. Touching Isaiah's lips with one cleanses him.

culture.title: The stump of a tree
culture.text: Terebinths and oaks, when cut down, can sprout again from the stump—a "holy seed" remains.

Isaiah 7.audience: Isaiah meets King Ahaz as Syria and Israel attack Judah, around 735 BC (Isaiah 7:1–2). Matthew quotes verse 14 of Jesus' birth (Matthew 1:23).

culture.title: The conduit of the upper pool
culture.text: Ahaz was probably inspecting Jerusalem's water supply in preparation for siege.

culture.title: Butter and honey
culture.text: Curds and wild honey were the food of a land returned to pasture after invasion, when fields could not be farmed.

culture.title: A hired razor
culture.text: God will shave Judah with "a razor that is hired"—the king of Assyria, whom Ahaz paid for help (2 Kings 16:7–8). Shaving a man was a deep humiliation.

Isaiah 8.audience: Isaiah's son Mahershalalhashbaz is named as a sign that Damascus and Samaria will soon fall to Assyria (Isaiah 8:3–4).

culture.title: Writing on a large tablet
culture.text: Isaiah writes the name on a large scroll or tablet "with a man's pen," in ordinary letters anyone could read, and has it witnessed.

culture.title: The waters of Shiloah
culture.text: Shiloah was the gently flowing water from the Gihon spring, contrasted with the flood of the Euphrates (Assyria).

culture.title: Wizards that peep and mutter
culture.text: Mediums spoke in whispering, chirping voices, supposedly from the dead.

Isaiah 9.audience: Isaiah speaks of light coming to Galilee, the region first devastated by Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Matthew quotes verses 1–2 of Jesus' ministry there (Matthew 4:14–16).

culture.title: Galilee of the nations
culture.text: Zebulun and Naphtali in Galilee were the first territories taken by Tiglathpileser, whose people were carried captive to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29).

culture.title: Garments rolled in blood
culture.text: Soldiers' boots and bloodied cloaks are burned after victory—a picture of war ended.

culture.title: Throne titles
culture.text: Egyptian and other kings received several throne names at their coronation. The child is given four: Wonderful Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

Isaiah 10.audience: Isaiah describes Assyria as the rod of God's anger and traces its army's advance toward Jerusalem town by town (Isaiah 10:28–32).

culture.title: Assyrian boasting
culture.text: Assyrian kings boasted in their inscriptions of the cities they had conquered—Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Damascus, Samaria. Isaiah quotes the same kind of boast.

culture.title: The axe boasting against the woodcutter
culture.text: A tool cannot boast against the one who uses it; Assyria is only God's instrument.

Isaiah 11.audience: Isaiah describes a ruler from "the stem of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:1), David's father. Paul quotes verse 10 in Romans 15:12.

culture.title: A shoot from a stump
culture.text: A tree cut down may send up a new shoot from its roots—a picture of David's line renewed after it seemed cut off.

culture.title: Predators and prey
culture.text: Wolves, leopards, lions, bears, and venomous snakes all lived in the land and threatened flocks and children.

culture.title: An ensign to the nations
culture.text: A banner raised on a hill signaled troops or people to gather.

Isaiah 12.audience: A short song of praise to be sung "in that day" by the restored people.

culture.title: Wells of salvation
culture.text: "With joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation." In later Jewish practice, water drawn from Siloam was poured out at the feast of tabernacles.

Isaiah 13.audience: Isaiah 13 begins the oracles against the nations (Isaiah 13–23), starting with Babylon. In Isaiah's day Babylon was a city under Assyrian rule; it later destroyed Jerusalem.

culture.title: The Medes
culture.text: The Medes, from what is now northwestern Iran, joined the Persians under Cyrus to conquer Babylon in 539 BC.

culture.title: Wild beasts in the ruins
culture.text: Abandoned cities became the home of desert animals and owls—a common curse on enemy cities.

Isaiah 14.audience: Isaiah gives a taunt song against the king of Babylon, who falls to the grave, and adds oracles against Assyria and Philistia.

culture.title: Lucifer, son of the morning
culture.text: "Lucifer" is the Latin name for the morning star (the planet Venus). The king who aimed to rise above the stars is brought down.

culture.title: The mount of the congregation
culture.text: "The sides of the north" echoes Canaanite belief in Zaphon, the mountain of the gods' assembly.

culture.title: Kings in their tombs
culture.text: Kings were buried with honor in their own tombs; to be left unburied was the greatest disgrace.

Isaiah 15.audience: An oracle about Moab, Judah's neighbor east of the Dead Sea, naming its towns—Ar, Kir, Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon.

culture.title: Baldness and cut beards
culture.text: Mourners shaved their heads and beards and wore sackcloth.

culture.title: Dibon
culture.text: Dibon was a Moabite town; the Moabite Stone, set up by King Mesha, was found there.

Isaiah 16.audience: The oracle on Moab continues, with Moabite refugees seeking shelter in Judah.

culture.title: Sending a lamb as tribute
culture.text: Moab had once paid tribute in lambs to Israel's king (2 Kings 3:4).

culture.title: Vines of Sibmah
culture.text: Moab's vineyards were famous. The joy of the grape harvest and the shouts of those treading the winepresses are silenced.

Isaiah 17.audience: An oracle against Damascus and Ephraim (Israel), allies against Judah. Assyria destroyed Damascus in 732 BC.

culture.title: Gleaning an olive tree
culture.text: After olives were beaten from the tree, a few were left at the top for the poor to glean—a picture of a small remnant.

culture.title: Groves and images
culture.text: Asherah poles (groves) and incense altars (images) were objects of Canaanite worship.

Isaiah 18.audience: An oracle about Ethiopia (Cush), the land south of Egypt along the Nile. Cushite kings ruled Egypt in Isaiah's day.

culture.title: Vessels of bulrushes
culture.text: Papyrus boats were used on the Nile, light and fast.

culture.title: A people tall and smooth
culture.text: Cushites were known as tall and smooth-skinned; Herodotus also described them as the tallest of men.

Isaiah 19.audience: An oracle about Egypt, which Judah's leaders were tempted to rely on against Assyria.

culture.title: The Nile dried up
culture.text: Egypt depended on the Nile for fishing, papyrus, and the flax used for linen. A failed river meant ruin for fishermen and weavers.

culture.title: Zoan and Noph
culture.text: Zoan (Tanis) and Noph (Memphis) were royal cities of Egypt.

culture.title: An altar in Egypt
culture.text: Isaiah foresees an altar to the LORD in Egypt. A Jewish temple later stood at Elephantine, and another at Leontopolis.

Isaiah 20.audience: In the year Assyria's commander took Ashdod (711 BC), Isaiah walks barefoot and stripped for three years as a sign against trusting Egypt and Ethiopia (Isaiah 20:1–3).

culture.title: Captives led naked
culture.text: Assyrian reliefs show prisoners led away barefoot and stripped—the humiliation Isaiah acts out.

culture.title: Tartan and Sargon
culture.text: "Tartan" is the title of Assyria's chief commander. Sargon II is named only here in the Bible; his own records describe the capture of Ashdod.

Isaiah 21.audience: Oracles about Babylon ("the desert of the sea"), Dumah (Edom), and Arabia.

culture.title: A watchman on the tower
culture.text: Watchmen stood on towers to report approaching riders—here chariots of horsemen, donkeys, and camels bringing news.

culture.title: Anoint the shield
culture.text: Leather shields were oiled to keep them supple before battle.

culture.title: Caravans of Dedan
culture.text: Dedan and Tema were Arabian oasis towns on the incense trade routes.

Isaiah 22.audience: An oracle against "the valley of vision"—Jerusalem itself—celebrating while danger approached. It names two officials of Hezekiah's court, Shebna and Eliakim.

culture.title: Breaking down houses for the wall
culture.text: Houses were torn down to strengthen the city wall against siege. A section of a thick wall in Jerusalem, the "Broad Wall," was built through earlier houses in Hezekiah's time.

culture.title: A tomb cut in the rock
culture.text: Shebna carves himself a grand tomb. A rock-cut tomb inscription in Silwan, Jerusalem, names a royal steward whose name ends in -yahu; some identify him with Shebna.

culture.title: The key of the house of David
culture.text: The steward carried the palace keys, a sign of authority. Revelation 3:7 applies "the key of David" to Christ.

Isaiah 23.audience: An oracle against Tyre and Sidon, the great Phoenician trading cities, whose ships sailed to Tarshish and Chittim (Cyprus).

culture.title: Seventy years
culture.text: Tyre will be forgotten seventy years, "according to the days of one king"—a normal lifetime.

culture.title: The merchants of the world
culture.text: Tyre's merchants were princes; Phoenicians founded trading colonies across the Mediterranean, including Carthage.

Isaiah 24.audience: Isaiah 24–27 turns from particular nations to judgment on the whole earth and a feast for all peoples on Mount Zion.

culture.title: The everlasting covenant broken
culture.text: The earth is defiled because its people have "broken the everlasting covenant"—recalling God's covenant with Noah and all humanity (Genesis 9:16).

culture.title: A lodge swaying
culture.text: The earth reels "like a drunkard" and sways "like a cottage"—a flimsy watchman's hut in a field.

Isaiah 25.audience: A song of praise for God's victory and a promise of a feast for all peoples. Paul quotes verse 8, "He will swallow up death in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54).

culture.title: A feast of fat things
culture.text: "Fat things full of marrow" and "wines on the lees well refined" describe the richest foods of a royal banquet.

culture.title: The veil over the nations
culture.text: Mourners covered their faces. God removes the covering of grief from all nations.

Isaiah 26.audience: A song to be sung in the land of Judah, celebrating a strong city and trust in God. Verse 19 speaks of the dead rising.

culture.title: A strong city with walls of salvation
culture.text: City walls and bulwarks (earthworks) were the main defense of ancient towns.

culture.title: Dew of herbs
culture.text: Dew revives plants in the dry season—an image for the dead coming to life.

Isaiah 27.audience: Isaiah describes God's victory over leviathan and the regathering of Israel from Assyria and Egypt.

culture.title: Leviathan the serpent
culture.text: Texts from Ugarit describe Baal defeating Lotan, ‘the twisting serpent’—nearly the same words Isaiah uses for leviathan.

culture.title: A great trumpet
culture.text: A great shofar blast summons exiles from Assyria and Egypt to worship in Jerusalem.

Isaiah 28.audience: Isaiah warns "the drunkards of Ephraim" (Samaria) and the scoffing rulers of Jerusalem. Paul and Peter quote verse 16 (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6).

culture.title: A crown of pride
culture.text: Samaria sat on a hill like a garland on a drunkard's head at a feast.

culture.title: Precept upon precept
culture.text: In Hebrew the words sound like baby talk or a child's spelling lesson—tsav latsav, kav lakav—the scoffers mocking Isaiah's teaching.

culture.title: The farmer's methods
culture.text: Different crops were threshed differently—fitches and cummin beaten with a rod, grain with a threshing sledge—each according to its kind.

Isaiah 29.audience: Isaiah speaks of Ariel—Jerusalem, "the city where David dwelt" (Isaiah 29:1). Jesus quotes verse 13 (Matthew 15:8–9).

culture.title: Ariel
culture.text: Ariel may mean ‘altar hearth’ (as in Ezekiel 43:15) or ‘lion of God.’

culture.title: A sealed book
culture.text: Scrolls were sealed with clay. A sealed book cannot be read by the literate, and the illiterate cannot read it at all.

culture.title: Potter and clay
culture.text: A potter shapes clay on a wheel; the clay cannot question the potter (Romans 9:20–21).

Isaiah 30.audience: Isaiah condemns Judah's envoys who travel to Egypt for help against Assyria. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities (Isaiah 30:4).

culture.title: Treasure on donkeys and camels
culture.text: Judah's envoys carry treasure through the dangerous Negev to buy Egypt's help.

culture.title: Rahab sitting still
culture.text: Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt; Isaiah calls it, in effect, ‘Rahab who sits still’—a monster that does nothing.

culture.title: Tophet
culture.text: Tophet was the place in the valley of Hinnom where children were burned to Molech (2 Kings 23:10). Here it is prepared for the king of Assyria.

Isaiah 31.audience: Isaiah warns again against relying on Egypt's horses and chariots and promises that the LORD will defend Jerusalem.

culture.title: Horses and chariots of Egypt
culture.text: Egypt was famous for its chariot forces and horses, and kings bought them from there (1 Kings 10:28).

culture.title: A lion over its prey
culture.text: Shepherds shouting together could not drive a lion from its prey.

Isaiah 32.audience: Isaiah describes a king who will reign in righteousness and warns the women of Jerusalem who are at ease.

culture.title: The shadow of a great rock
culture.text: In the desert, the shade of a large rock gives relief from the burning sun.

culture.title: Beating the breasts
culture.text: Women beat their breasts in mourning for lost fields and vines.

Isaiah 33.audience: Isaiah addresses a destroyer who will be destroyed and describes Jerusalem at peace, a city of quiet habitation.

culture.title: Ambassadors weeping
culture.text: Envoys sent to make peace return weeping—treaties broken (compare 2 Kings 18:14–17).

culture.title: Tent stakes and cords
culture.text: Jerusalem is pictured as a tent whose stakes will never be pulled up nor its cords broken.
